clue.text: Lag once around a tank, one hollow

indicators.note: to be around something is to surround it, so one piece wraps the others

parts.note: a lag is a convict, and one who was a lag once is a former convict
taken as written
a vat is a large tank for liquids
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A former prisoner wanders round a big tank, feeling empty inside.
explanation.walkthrough: Lag is British slang for a convict, so 'once' makes him a former one. 'Hollow' looks like an adjective, but it is a noun here.
explanation.definitionFit: An excavation is a dug-out pit or cavity, and a hollow is likewise a sunken space in the ground.

clue.text: Burn fine shed within reach

indicators.note: to shed something is to cast it off, so a letter is dropped from the word that follows

parts.note: to fetch a place is to arrive at or reach it, and an item fetches a price it reaches
F is the pencil-grade abbreviation for fine

explanation.surface: Someone sets fire to a fine little shed that stands close at hand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fine shed' reads as a building, but shed is a verb: F is cast off from FETCH, leaving ETCH.
explanation.definitionFit: Etching uses acid to eat into a metal plate, so the acid burns the design into the surface.

clue.text: Nobleman upset excellent fellows in deeply personal retort

parts.note: a count is a European noble title

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset means tipped upside down, so the letters read from bottom to top

parts.note: rare can mean unusually good, as in a rare treat

indicators.note: one thing placed in another sits inside it, so these letters go into the next piece

parts.note: a gut feeling is instinctive and intimately one's own
fellows are men

explanation.surface: A disgruntled aristocrat answers some fine chaps with a very personal put-down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' looks like the nobleman's mood, but it turns the next piece over. Rare meaning excellent is an old-fashioned sense, as in 'a rare old time'.
explanation.definitionFit: A retort is a sharp reply made against what someone said, which is exactly what an opposing point in debate is.

clue.text: Criminal's country house home

parts.note: a villa is a large house in the country
someone who is home is in

explanation.surface: A gangster's possessions: a country house he calls home.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s reads as possessive, but it stands for 'is', linking the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A villain is a wrongdoer, a common British term for a crook or lawbreaker.

clue.text: Burning awful endless rubbish that's turned up

indicators.note: without an end means the final letter is lopped off
in a down clue, turning something up makes it read from bottom to top

parts.note: awful is DIRE, losing its final letter
rot is nonsense or rubbish

explanation.surface: A dreadful, never-ending heap of rubbish is set alight and smoulders.
explanation.walkthrough: DIR plus ROT gives DIRROT, which read upwards becomes TORRID.
explanation.definitionFit: Torrid describes scorching heat, as in a torrid desert climate, so it matches intensely hot weather.

clue.text: Figures leave cats on crumpled covers

indicators.note: to cover is to lie over and enclose, so one piece wraps another
something crumpled has been squashed out of shape, so its letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written, as letters to rearrange
to leave is to go

explanation.surface: Some people leave the house when cats settle on the crumpled bedcovers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leave' is not a verb to obey but a word to replace: GO sits inside a rearrangement of CATS ON.
explanation.definitionFit: Octagons are eight-sided shapes, and geometric shapes are called figures in mathematics.

clue.text: Girl cut husband's fine hair

indicators.note: a word that is cut short loses its last letter

parts.note: a girl is a lass, here docked of its final letter
H is the standard abbreviation for husband

explanation.surface: A young woman trims her husband's thin hair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut' looks like the hairdresser's job, but it trims the girl. Lass is the British and Scottish word for a girl.
explanation.definitionFit: An eyelash is one of the slender short hairs fringing the eyelid, so a fine hair is fair.

clue.text: Everyone rushed after dawn to get menu offering

parts.note: everyone is all
daybreak is dawn
rushed in the sense of quick

explanation.surface: Everyone hurried out at first light to get something to eat at a cafe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' places the rushed piece behind dawn. An all-day breakfast is a British cafe staple: a fried breakfast served at any hour.
explanation.definitionFit: Cafes list a full fried morning meal available at any time of day as an item to order.

clue.text: Antelope can't stand crossing river, most advantageous to traverse end of June

indicators.note: to cross something here is to straddle it, so one piece is held across another

parts.note: to be unable to stand something is to hate it
R is the map abbreviation for river

indicators.note: to traverse is to stretch across, so one piece spans and encloses the next

parts.note: the most advantageous option is the best

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the month

explanation.surface: An antelope that dislikes water must pick the best time to ford a river, around late June.
explanation.walkthrough: HATE holds R to make HARTE, and BEST spans E to make BEEST.
explanation.definitionFit: The hartebeest is a large African grassland antelope with a long face and curved horns.

clue.text: Rising alert, cover removed and connecting device

indicators.note: removing a cover strips the outside, so the first and last letters go

parts.note: a rising, as in an uprising, is a coup
alert with its outer letters taken away

explanation.surface: A rising alarm, a cover taken off, and some piece of connecting equipment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rising' looks like a reversal signal, but it is a noun meaning a revolt.
explanation.definitionFit: A coupler is a link that joins two parts, such as railway carriages or pipes, together.

clue.text: Truck seen outside large boozer

indicators.note: a thing seen outside another surrounds it, so one piece wraps the other

parts.note: a tipper is a dump truck that tips its load
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: A lorry is parked outside a big pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boozer' is British slang for a pub, which is the picture the surface paints; here it means a drinker.
explanation.definitionFit: A tippler is a habitual drinker, and boozer in its other sense is a heavy drinker.

clue.text: Stick of crayon with end snapped off

indicators.note: snapping off the end of something leaves it one letter shorter at the tail

parts.note: a pastel is a stick of coloured chalk, a kind of crayon

explanation.surface: A broken stick of crayon, its tip snapped off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stick' looks like a noun describing the crayon, but it is a verb and the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To paste something is to glue it down, so it is a direct synonym of the verb to stick.

clue.text: Firm area tasted great in bananas

indicators.note: going bananas means going crazy, so these letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written, as letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Somewhere solid tasted wonderful in a banana dessert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Area' looks like part of the fodder, but it belongs to the definition. A trading estate is the British term for a business park.
explanation.definitionFit: A trading estate is a zone of land set aside for businesses, so it is an area for firms.

clue.text: Grand supermarket to the north invested in new cooks and food taster

parts.note: G is short for grand, a thousand

indicators.note: in a down clue, heading north means reading upwards, so the letters run backwards
to be invested in something is to be put inside it, so one piece goes into another
a new version is remade, so these letters take a fresh order

parts.note: taken as written, as letters to rearrange
Lidl is a German discount supermarket chain common across Europe

explanation.surface: A major supermarket chain up north has put money into new chefs and a professional food taster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Invested' reads as money, but it means placed inside. In a down clue, 'to the north' means the letters read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: In the fairy tale, Goldilocks samples the three bears' porridge, so she is literally a taster of food.

clue.text: Rowing and shouting without introduction

indicators.note: lacking its introduction means the opening letter is missing

parts.note: roaring is loud shouting

explanation.surface: A crew rows hard while yelling, nobody having been introduced.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rowing' could be the British sense of quarrelling, which fits the shouting; it is the boating sense here.
explanation.definitionFit: Oaring is propelling a boat with oars, a literary synonym for the boating sense of rowing.

clue.text: Sample of children's emblemed outfit

indicators.note: a sample is a small portion taken from a larger whole, so the letters come from inside the words

parts.note: running across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A sample of a children's uniform with a badge sewn on.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across the apostrophe and word break, from the tail of the first word into the second.
explanation.definitionFit: An ensemble is a complete coordinated set of clothes worn together, the fashion sense of outfit.

clue.text: Comedian and DJ in Lebanese city

parts.note: an MC is a rapper or DJ who works a crowd
taken as written
Tyre is an ancient port city in southern Lebanon

explanation.surface: A stand-up and a DJ are performing in a city in Lebanon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a container signal but is simply its own letters, placed between the other two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Michael McIntyre is a hugely popular British stand-up comic and television presenter.

clue.text: Tone in discord with such inactivity might be condemnatory

indicators.note: things in discord are out of harmony, so the letters fall out of order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, as letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A disapproving tone towards someone's idleness might come across as condemning.
explanation.walkthrough: A compound anagram: TONE plus the answer, jumbled, make CONDEMNATORY, so remove TONE's letters from it and rearrange the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Dormancy is a state of being asleep or inert, as with a dormant volcano or seed, hence a lack of action.

clue.text: Shelled cashew nuts primarily pale

indicators.note: a shelled nut has lost its casing, so the outermost letters are stripped away

parts.note: the inside of the word once its first and last letters are gone

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so only the opening letter is kept

parts.note: the opening letter

explanation.surface: Shelled cashews are mostly a pale colour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Primarily' looks like it means mostly, but it picks the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Ashen describes a face drained of colour, grey like ash, so it means pale or wan.

clue.text: Doubts persist regularly and dominate

indicators.note: at regular intervals means every other letter is kept

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth letters and so on

explanation.surface: Recurring doubts keep coming back and take over one's mind.
explanation.walkthrough: Take every second letter across both words, starting with the second letter of the first.
explanation.definitionFit: When a thought obsesses someone it preoccupies their mind completely, so it controls or rules their thinking.

clue.text: Online account provider

parts.note: surface reading: an internet bank or email service that opens accounts for customers
setter's reading: a person who writes accounts, in the sense of stories, posted on the web

explanation.walkthrough: 'Account' suggests banking or a login, but an account is also a written narrative of events.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who keeps a web diary publishes written reports of their experiences for readers on the internet.

clue.text: A starter of salmon on board in canteen is wrong

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: a starter comes first, so only the opening letter is kept

parts.note: the opening letter
a tray is the flat board you carry food on in a canteen

explanation.surface: Serving salmon as a starter on the menu in a works canteen is a mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starter' looks like a first course, but it selects a first letter. In a down clue, 'on' puts the earlier pieces above the board.
explanation.definitionFit: To go astray is to go off course or into error, so the adverb means awry or wrong.

clue.text: Spooner's putting personnel in part of canal, silly person

indicators.note: Spooner was famous for swapping the opening sounds of words, so initial sounds trade places

parts.note: putting personnel in place is staffing; trading its opening S sound for the other word's L, it is said 'laffing'
a lock is the gated section of a canal; taking the S sound in place of its L, it is said 'stock'

explanation.surface: A warden staffs a canal lock with people, one of them a fool.
explanation.walkthrough: STAFFING LOCK, with the opening sounds swapped, becomes LAFFING STOCK.
explanation.definitionFit: A laughing stock is someone made an object of ridicule, so a foolish figure everyone mocks.

clue.text: Group listened to broadcast

indicators.note: something broadcast goes out over the airwaves for an audience, so a word is taken by its sound rather than its spelling

parts.note: listened to is heard, and sounds identical

explanation.surface: A band were heard on the radio.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Group' suggests a pop band, but here it is a herd of animals.
explanation.definitionFit: A herd is a collection of animals such as cattle moving together, so it is a kind of group.

clue.text: Knight ousting king, evidently without hindrance

indicators.note: to oust is to push out and take the place of, so one letter replaces another

parts.note: evidently means clearly
N is the chess notation for knight
R is for Rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: A chess knight takes a king and moves freely.
explanation.walkthrough: The chess picture is apt, since N is knight in chess notation, but the king to be ousted is R for Rex, not K.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something cleanly means smoothly with no snags, such as a ball struck cleanly or a clean getaway.

clue.text: Exposed area reportedly became dull and rank again

indicators.note: something exposed has its covering removed, so the outer letters go

parts.note: the word stripped of its first and last letters

indicators.note: what is reported is passed on by word of mouth, so we go by sound

parts.note: a sky that became dull greyed over

explanation.surface: An open patch of land reportedly turned drab and smelly again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rank' sounds like smelly, which suits the dull area, but it is a verb meaning to grade.
explanation.definitionFit: To regrade is to assign a new grade or level, which is to rank something a second time.

clue.text: I'm hesitant to leave dog home

indicators.note: what leaves departs, so those letters drop out of the word

parts.note: a setter is a breed of gun dog
er is the sound of someone hesitating

explanation.surface: Someone is reluctant to leave the dog at home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I'm hesitant' is not the speaker's mood but the hesitation sound itself, which leaves the dog.
explanation.definitionFit: A sett is the burrow where a badger lives, so it is that animal's home.

clue.text: Dead dry, the ground lacking water

indicators.note: something ground is crushed to bits, so the letters are broken up and reassembled

parts.note: taken as written, as letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: The earth is bone dry, with no water in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ground' looks like the parched earth in the picture, but it is a past participle signalling the jumble.
explanation.definitionFit: Something dehydrated has had its moisture removed, so it is without fluid, like dried fruit.
